claims.text: Typical bulk HfNbTaTiZr contains inherent lattice distortions and processing-related defects.
A first-principles approach augmented with experimentally calibrated machine-learning corrections will be more accurate than ideal, defect-free analytical models.
The proposed accuracy advantage will apply to HfNbTaTiZr in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Correction factors calibrated with defect and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen data can account for their effects on HfNbTaTiZr conductivity.
Defect-induced ionized-impurity scattering dominates conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr from nearly 0 to 200 K.
Electron–phonon interactions dominate conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr from 300 to 1200 K.
Compositional disorder and atomic-size mismatch produce displacement disorder that changes electronic relaxation and scattering.
Oxygen-related defects modify local electronic states or bonding and thereby affect conductivity.
Machine-learning corrections trained on experimental conductivity data can embed the influence of non-ideal structural features in first-principles predictions.
Thermally activated carrier mobility is an important high-temperature conductivity mechanism in HfNbTaTiZr.
Relative to a perfect-crystal model, the corrected model will predict lower conductivity at 0–200 K because of enhanced impurity scattering.
Relative to a perfect-crystal model, the corrected model will predict a moderated conductivity increase at 300–1200 K.
The combined method will improve predictive accuracy by more than approximately 20%.
Existing ideal-crystal analytical approaches typically overestimate HfNbTaTiZr conductivity because they omit scattering from imperfections and oxygen.
The proposed approach is applicable from 0 to 1200 K to samples containing around 1 wt.% oxygen.
The magnitude of the accuracy improvement will depend on defect-distribution variability and the size and representativeness of the calibration dataset.

contradictions.description: The conditions define two evaluated regimes, 0–200 K and 300–1200 K, leaving 200–300 K unaddressed, whereas the boundary claims applicability over the continuous range 0–1200 K.
